projects.headline: On the Digilent Nexys A7-100T (xc7a100tcsg324-1, Vivado 2026.1) the on-chip checker caught each of the 6 protocol bugs we seeded, on the board, by the rule it breaks; against our own peripheral and stream FIFO, the board's traffic matched simulation cycle for cycle in 13 of 13 runs.

agent.plan: The owner chose the project and set the rules; a planner session wrote the brief; an AI executor (a language-model coding agent) wrote the RTL, the rule monitors (from the specification, in its own words), the seeded bugs, the proofs, the simulation and the board runs. The bugs were seeded by the same executor that wrote the checker; the AMD checker is the part it did not write.
agent.request: The owner asked for an on-chip AMBA AXI transactor and analyser that exercises on-chip modules with transactions of any complexity while verifying protocol correctness.

story.how: A transaction program, written in plain YAML and loaded over the serial link, drives AXI4-Lite and AXI4-Stream traffic with seeded random addresses, data, byte-enables, pauses by the sender and refusals by the receiver. Monitors that watch only the bus wires check 9 AXI4-Lite and 5 AXI4-Stream rules every cycle. A reference copy of the memory checks every read, counters record latency, stalls and which cases were covered, and the first violation starts a capture. The same program runs on the board and in simulation.
story.problem: A bus interface that breaks the AXI handshake rules often passes a quick test and fails in a system: read data that is not held while the master stalls, or a write response sent before the data. Such bugs show only under the right timing, and a logic analyser shows the waveform but not which rule it breaks. The hard part is the checker, not the traffic: a wrong checker passes bad designs or flags good ones, so this one is checked formally, attacked with deliberately broken copies of itself, and compared with AMD's own checker. Making the board and the simulation see identical traffic is the other hard part: every random choice has to be seeded.
results: 17 board runs, fixed in a written plan before the board was used: 6 with a seeded protocol bug, 2 with a seeded data bug, 9 clean. All 17 gave the expected verdict.

Each protocol bug was flagged by exactly the rule it breaks. The data bugs (write byte-enables ignored, the end-of-packet marker TLAST lost) were caught by the reference memory or the stream receiver alone, and all 9 clean runs fired nothing. A demonstration on bugs we planted, not a measure of coverage.

Board against simulation, for our own peripheral and stream FIFO: a checksum over every transaction, including its latency in cycles, and the run's length in cycles were identical in 13 of 13 runs; 0 of 936 logged transactions differed.
Independent check: AMD's AXI Protocol Checker, watching the same bus, raised its flag in exactly the 5 runs where ours flagged an AXI4-Lite rule; the two agree in 17 of 17 runs.

The checker is formally checked to a limited depth: 30 of 30 proofs over 20 clock cycles show each rule quiet on legal traffic and firing on its own seeded violation, and 34 of 34 deliberately broken copies of the checker were caught. The properties were written by the same author as the checker, which is why the AMD checker matters.

Against AMD's AXI BRAM Controller, under random back-pressure, write latency ran from 2 to 12 cycles and read latency from 1 to 8; 107 reads were checked against the reference memory with no mismatch.

The whole board design used 7089 LUTs and met timing with 0.188 ns of slack; Vivado estimated 0.189 W. Measured on the die: at most 27.32 C, core supply rail (VCCINT) from 1.0042 to 1.0071 V, inside the recommended operating conditions, 0 alarms latched.

projects.one_line: Ask for a capture in words, such as "show me the UART byte when the FIFO overflows": the agent picks the signals by their RTL names, sets the trigger, rebuilds with a logic analyser, captures on the board and answers in plain words beside the waveform.
